subtitle: "Appendix · common English phrases by section and by situation"
date: last-modified
---

Use this page when you get stuck on wording. It is based on the lab's [Lab Manager phrase list](https://github.com/kkonoo/lab-manager/blob/main/tips/phrases.md) (in Korean), revised to fit the principles of this course.

- Do not paste a phrase as it is. Adapt it to your results and to the strength of your evidence.
- Square brackets `[ ]` mark what you fill in with your own content.
- Use stock phrases once or twice in a whole manuscript at most. The standard is pattern 10 of [W3](chapters/w03_readable_sentences.qmd).
- The numbers in the examples come from the course's shared fictional example study.

# By section {#by-section}

## Introduction {#introduction}

The full structure is in [W9](chapters/w09_introduction.qmd).

| What you want to say | Phrases |
|---|---|
| First sentence: a fact readers can check | [Disease] affects more than [number] people worldwide [ref]. / [X] is a leading cause of [outcome] [ref]. |
| Accumulated evidence | Recent studies have shown that [finding] [refs]. |
| What is not known (gap) | However, it is not known whether [question]. / The mechanism by which [X] [does Y] remains unclear. |
| This study | Here, we tested whether [question] in [model]. / In this study, we asked whether [question]. |
| Summary of this study (if the journal wants it) | We show that [main finding]. |

- "plays a crucial role" and "has attracted increasing attention" are stock phrases with nothing to check. Put a number or a fact there instead.
- Claim a gap only as far as you searched. Write "No study has examined …" only when your search log supports it.

## Methods {#methods}

Past tense is the default. Match the voice to the journal and the sentence. The full standard is in [W5](chapters/w05_methods_legends.qmd).

| What you want to say | Phrases |
|---|---|
| Animals and treatment | Male C57BL/6J mice (8 weeks old) underwent left UUO. / Compound X (10 mg/kg) or vehicle was given by oral gavage once daily from day 0 to day 6. |
| Randomization, blinding | Mice were randomly assigned to [groups]. The person who quantified [outcome] was blinded to group. |
| Citing an earlier method | [Method] was performed as previously described [ref], with the following changes: [changes]. |
| n and technical replicates | n = 6 mice per group. For each mouse, values from three sections were averaged. |
| Statistics | Data are presented as mean ± SD. Groups were compared by one-way ANOVA with Tukey's multiple comparisons test. |
| Software | Analyses were performed in [software, version]. |

- Do not write only "as previously described" and leave out what you changed. State the changes.
- Even if you write "P < 0.05 was considered significant", give exact P values in the text and figures.

## Figure legend {#legend}

The order is title, panel descriptions, then n and statistics. The example is the fictional Figure 2 in [W5](chapters/w05_methods_legends.qmd#principles).

| Slot | Phrases |
|---|---|
| Title sentence | Figure 2. Compound X reduces interstitial fibrosis after UUO. |
| Panel description | (a) Representative [stain] images of [tissue] from [groups] on day [n]. Scale bars, [length]. |
| What one dot is | Each dot is one mouse (mean of three sections). |
| Summary values and n | Bars show mean ± SD; n = 6 mice per group. |
| Test | P values are from [test]. |

- Do not interpret in the legend. Words such as "suggesting that it may be a promising therapy" belong in the Discussion.

## Results {#results}

A paragraph runs purpose, what was done, result, short interpretation ([W6](chapters/w06_results.qmd)).

| What you want to say | Phrases |
|---|---|
| Purpose and what was done | To test whether [question], we [method] (Fig. [n]). / We next asked whether [question]. |
| Increased | [X] increased [Y] from [a] to [b] ([statistics]; Fig. [n]). / … by [n]-fold |
| Decreased | [X] reduced (lowered) [Y] by [n]% compared with [control]. |
| No difference | [Y] did not differ between [groups] ([statistics]). |
| Dose or time dependence | [Y] decreased as the dose increased ([statistics]). |
| Short interpretation (its own sentence) | Thus, [X] reduced [Y] in [model]. / These results suggest that [interpretation]. |

- Use "significantly" only for a comparison you tested, and give the P value of that test.
- Do not attach the interpretation as ", suggesting that …". Write it as a separate sentence.
- Do not claim more causation than you tested in a Results sentence. Write "by blocking …" only if you tested it.

## Discussion {#discussion}

The first paragraph answers the question of the Introduction ([W10](chapters/w10_discussion.qmd)).

| What you want to say | Phrases |
|---|---|
| Main finding | We found that [main finding]. / Compound X reduced kidney fibrosis after UUO in mice. |
| Agrees with earlier work | This agrees with [Author et al.], who found [finding] in [model] [ref]. |
| Differs from earlier work | In contrast to [Author et al.] [ref], we observed [finding]. This difference may reflect [specific reason]. |
| Implication | These results raise the possibility that [implication]. |
| Limitation | We used only [condition], so [what we cannot conclude]. |
| Next step | [Specific experiment] would test whether [question]. |
| Last sentence | [One-sentence answer to the question of the Introduction]. |

- Do not write only "Further studies are needed". Say which experiment answers which question.
- Write only the limitations that apply to this study, together with their effect on the conclusion.
- Do not use "prove". Use "first" or "novel" only when your search log confirms it.

## Abstract and title {#abstract}

The five parts of the Abstract come from other parts of the manuscript ([W11](chapters/w11_abstract_title.qmd)).

| Part | Phrases |
|---|---|
| Background | [Disease or problem] [fact with number]. |
| Gap | Whether [question] is unknown. |
| Approach | Here, we [method] in [model; species; n]. |
| Key results | [X] reduced [Y] from [a] to [b] ([statistics]). |
| Conclusion | [X] [effect] in [model], which suggests [careful implication]. |

- To cut words, cut whole points, not articles, verbs or connectives.
- Write a result-type title (*Compound X reduces kidney fibrosis after ureteral obstruction in mice*), a descriptive one and a question, then choose. The verb of the title must not be stronger than the conclusion sentence of the Abstract.

# By situation {#by-situation}

## Verbs that match the strength of the evidence {#hedging}

The same standard as the hedging table in [W10](chapters/w10_discussion.qmd).

| Evidence | Phrases |
|---|---|
| Measured directly and tested | reduced, increased, did not change, showed |
| Changed together, cause not tested | was accompanied by, is associated with, suggests, indicates |
| Speculation beyond the data | may, might, one possibility is (in a separate sentence) |

- Do not stack hedges. "might potentially have a possible effect" blurs what you found.

## Numbers and comparisons {#numbers}

| What you want to say | Phrases |
|---|---|
| Range | from 18.2% to 9.6% |
| Reduced by a share | by 47% / a 47% reduction |
| Fold change | a 2.3-fold increase |
| Comparing two groups | compared with vehicle (use compared with for differences) |
| Matching order | A and B were 10 and 20, respectively. |
| Summary values | mean ± SD / median (interquartile range) |

## Connectives {#connectives}

| Meaning | Phrases |
|---|---|
| Adding | In addition, / Also, |
| Contrast | However, / In contrast, |
| Consequence | Therefore, / Thus, |
| Summary | Taken together, |

- "Notably", "Importantly" and "Interestingly" are common in AI text. Use them once or twice in a whole manuscript at most.
- If the meaning follows without a connective, you can leave it out.

# Submission and response {#submission}

## Cover letter {#cover-letter}

The structure and examples are in [W13](chapters/w13_submission.qmd).

| Slot | Phrases |
|---|---|
| First sentence | We submit our manuscript, "[Title]," for consideration as an [article type] in [Journal]. |
| Main results | In [model], [X] [result with the same numbers as the Abstract]. |
| Why this journal | [Journal] recently published [Author et al., Year, DOI], which [what it did]. Our study extends that work by [how]. |
| Required statements | This manuscript has not been published and is not under consideration elsewhere. All authors have approved the manuscript. |

- "novel and groundbreaking", "prestigious journal" and "perfect fit" are things an editor cannot check. Write facts.

## Response to reviewers {#response}

Answer each comment with quote, thanks, what you did, and where it changed ([W14](chapters/w14_reviewer_response.qmd)).

| Slot | Phrases |
|---|---|
| Thanks (one sentence) | We thank the reviewer for this suggestion. |
| What you did | We now show [what] (Fig. [n]). We also state in the Methods [what]. |
| Where it changed | Changes: [section], page [n], lines [n–n]. |
| When you do not accept | We did not [do X], because [evidence]. We now state this limitation in the Discussion (page [n], lines [n–n]). |
| When the reviewer misread | We have rewritten [section] to make clear that [point]. |

- Do not write analyses you did not do or promises you cannot keep.

## Disclosing AI use {#ai-disclosure}

If the journal gives a wording, use it. General examples are in [W2](chapters/w02_ai_basics.qmd).

- Acknowledgments (writing help): During the preparation of this manuscript, the authors used [tool name and version] to check grammar and improve the readability of the text. The authors reviewed and edited all suggested changes and take full responsibility for the content of the article.
- Methods (help with analysis code): We used [tool name and version] to help write the [language] code that [task]. The authors reviewed and tested all code before use.

# Easily confused words {#confusables}

| Confusion | Correct use |
|---|---|
| affect / effect | affect is a verb (to influence), effect is a noun (a result) |
| data is | data are (plural) |
| compared to / with | use compared with for differences |
| which / that | that (no comma) for essential information, ", which" for added information |
| i.e. / e.g. | i.e. means "that is", e.g. means "for example" |
| while / whereas | use whereas for contrast (while can be read as "during") |
| since / because | use because for reasons (since can be read as "after") |
| less / fewer | fewer cells (countable), less protein (uncountable) |

# Habits from Korean {#korean-habits}

| Avoid | Correct use |
|---|---|
| researches, informations, evidences | research, information, evidence (uncountable) |
| According to the result, … | These results indicate that … |
| very significantly, more significantly | Significance takes no degree adverb. Give the effect size and the P value |
| different with | different from |
| In this study in every paragraph | Once is enough |
| 10 mice were … (a number starting the sentence) | Ten mice were … |

- Articles: a/an for something new, the for something already mentioned or unique, no article for plural general statements (Cells were …).
- The translationese checklist is in [W12](chapters/w12_polishing.qmd).
